utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are present. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey today on his own. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Haynes. While I was making this statement, Mr. Mitchell for the Prosecution entered the courtroom. The witness is present. We are going to proceed and conclude with his testimony. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General Obradovic. Almost finished. Just a couple of -- two or three more intercepts that should be pretty quick. You had -- in talking about an intercept that Mr. Petrusic had showed you, there was a reference in it where General Miletic said he was not authorised to do something, and he had to check with his superior. I think we remember that. And I want to show you another intercept. It's 65 ter number 1401 B, and I'm handing you a copy, and A is in the English. And this is dated August 4th, and so I'm not so interested in the -- the overall content. We can see from this that this, according to the BiH army, is between General Miletic and a UN Colonel that they spell out as Quape. Do you remember a UN Colonel with a name like that that may have been in contact with the Main Staff at about this time-period? You can see briefly what it's about. General Miletic seems to be quite upset with this fellow over some shenanigans he felt that the UN was pulling in their -- UN in their convoys. Does that UN name bring back any memory?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not remember this name, Quape, that is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, maybe as you look at that you'll remember something about it, because I think you will agree with me that General Miletic is not happy with this colonel, and I just simply want to recall your attention to the -- I've marked with a pen on that paragraph, and it's the bottom paragraph in the English. So I think we are going to need to -- to go up. And it's -- it's about two-thirds of the way down in the B/C/S, and it starts out with: "No, sir, no..." This is General Miletic. And maybe you can help us. In that second line. There's this word that a helicopter had landed at, and then it's "inzjnjering" or something. Do you know what that word is? Our translation people didn't, where the helicopter was landing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that name. The meaning of the word "inzjnjering," "engineering," I would have to know the context to be sure what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And anyway, we see from this that the UN were allegedly shipping out some wounded, but General Miletic goes on and says: "And I have information that you are not carrying just those two, your wounded, and I have no desire whatsoever to take on any more responsibility myself, because at that time I approved it on my own responsibility, not with the agreement of my commander. I have no desire to take on that responsibility myself because of your improper behaviour. You may I have ground transport to Kiseljak, but you can set off whenever you like. Just say when you're setting off, and then you won't fool me again." Then they go on and talk a little bit more, mentioning Tolimir, Mladic, Smith, Janvier. So my question is, do you think General Miletic was telling truth to this colonel when he said that he authorised that movement of the wounded himself, or was that something you think he might have just been saying, you know, for the purpose of argument in influencing this colonel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, knowing General Miletic, I do not believe that he would engage in any kind of manipulation. I am not acquainted with this particular event, but if he did something on his own, against the regulations and then was reprimanded for it from his commander or the Main Staff, then I can understand his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you recall any time in August General Miletic being able to make these decisions about a transport, a UN transport, on his own?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not authorised to take such decisions himself. He always consulted the Chief of Staff or the commander to get certain approvals, and if he did something on his own for the benefit of the wounded and was fooled, then I understand his -- his mood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. All right. Let's go to the next one. When General Miletic was fooled or was angry, he was a force to be reckoned with, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was seldom angry. These are extraordinary circumstances. I, as his subordinate officer, in no contact with him saw him angry. He was always very calm and collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, that didn't answer my question, but I think we can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3911. This is dated August 7th, and I think it's that top one I put a little star by. Take a little time to read this one, because this has someone named Obradovic speaking, and in this intercept Obradovic seems to be answering the phone, and a Colonel Lazic asks for Miletic. Now, do you know a Colonel Lazic from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Lazic, I think his first name is Milan. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you talked to him at all this year?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen him since the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear that he testified in here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in this conversation it looks like Colonel Lazic is calling the Main Staff, and he gets you, and he says: "Hi, Obradovic" -- or you say: Yes, please, Lazic. Obradovic here, or, Here Obradovic. He says: "Hi, Obradovic." You say: "Hi. How are you?" He says: "Fine. Hey, is Miletic there?" And you say: "Miletic went down to Radovan's. Ah ha." Then you go on a little bit and talk about some things that I'm not really that interested in. I'm not sure there is any real reason for you to remember this conversation, but in looking at it, do you believe that this is you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when Colonel Lazic asks you where Miletic is, you said Miletic went down to Radovan's. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the corps commander; that is, to the zone of the Herzegovina Corps. And I identified the corps by mentioning the name of the corps commander, and that's Radovan Grubac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mention, actually, Grubac's -- or sorry, Colonel Lazic actually mentions Grubac's name later on. Okay. Thank you. There is this other person named Radovan that I just wanted to clear that one up. Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was misguided. He had said to me that he was in the west, and I was inquiring whether the roads were jammed by the large number of refugees. But he was, in fact, elsewhere, with the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you remember this situation that you gentlemen are talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many conversations. I can identify this. I am sure this is me and Colonel Lazic, but I'm -- wouldn't know about the details. There were many conversations. You can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Colonel from the Drina Corps that I am talking about is named Milenko Lazic. Is that the one you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then the -- I believe the last - I hope the last - intercept is 65 ter 3917, and it's a bit of a long one. It's dated 3 September 1995, and it starts out at 1311.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you look at the bottom of that first page, that's where the conversation starts at 1311. And, again, I'm really not that concerned about the content of this long conversation, but it again appears to be involving you, and as we see from this, it looks like Karadzic calls and announces himself over the open air waves as Karadzic speaking. You say: "Good afternoon. Colonel Obradovic. Can I help you, President?" So I take it as you have called him "President," this is the President Karadzic that's here in Scheveningen at the moment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the first thing he asks you is: "Where is General Miletic?" And you say: "He went down to the barracks. He told me that he's on his way, but he's not in the building yet." Do you know what you mean when you say this to the president, which barracks, which building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facility at Crna Rijeka was at the foot of the Zepa mountain. We stayed at the facilities there when there were no threats from NATO that they would bomb us. When we thought that they could bomb us, they -- we would do something else. We would go to an underground facility at the foot of the Zepa mountain. We had lots of personal things. General Miletic went to fetch some things there, and in the meantime the -- the president called, and he excepted General Miletic to answer the phone, and Miletic left me behind to answer the phones in case there would -- in case someone would call, and he had left. The distance between us was some 2, 2 and a half kilometres, but it is all the command post at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's a pretty good example of why it's important for Miletic to let people know where he is when he leaves the building.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the duty of a superior officer, a commanding officer [as interpreted], but he doesn't -- he doesn't give this information to many people. He just informs me so that I know what to do when someone wants to contact him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in line 17 on page 7, up until "commanding officer." Well, "commanding officer" was not the phrase the witness used. He said, in fact, a "superior officer." I suggest that this be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is already "superior officer." What I think you are suggesting is the deletion from the transcript of the words "commanding officer" then, yes? I need to check with the witness and also with the interpreters, what they heard, please. It seems to be superior officer for sure, but did the witness also say "commanding officer"? Can someone help me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said "superior officer," and that applies to all levels. The superior officer informs the person standing in for him, where he is going, for how long he will be absent, and how he can be reached when the official need arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then after -- well, let me ask you, do you remember where you were when you picked up the phone? Were you in Miletic's office, Milovanovic's office, the ops room?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miletic's office door was open, and I heard the phone, and I was in the ops room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then the president, his next person he wants to talk -- he says: "Is Mladic somewhere close by?" And you say: "No, he went on a trip this morning." And then can the Karadzic says: "Uh-huh. He went far, right?" -- going over to the next page in the English. Was that true? Had General Mladic gone someplace far that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he had left that day. I said that he had left. I think that he went west.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Is it possible that Mladic is there and he had just told you guys that if the president calls, tell him that I'm not around?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When -- I'm sure you're familiar in August when President Karadzic tried to fire General Mladic, right? It's public.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't try to fire him. I believe that he appointed him as his advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Even worse. Okay. Well, be it fire or his advisor, as you know, many generals in the VRS signed or were against that. And can you tell us, you must know where General Miletic stood on that. Did he -- was he against President Karadzic's move towards Mladic on that regard? Or did he support it or stay neutral?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic didn't discuss that with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, must know where he stood on that issue of all issues. Even if he didn't discuss it with you, what's --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know his position based on that list and his signature, but he didn't speak to me about that, the list of persons supporting the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you saw the list of people supporting a commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you just referred to it. Do you know if Miletic was on that list or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned it from the media. Nobody ever showed me the list because I believe that the signatories didn't sign it all at once, but the general public knew the positions of the generals with regard to that initiative of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So to your knowledge, what you learned in the media was General Miletic, had he signed off on that list supporting Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, a majority or nearly all generals signed that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's right, and I'm sure you would remember whether or not General Miletic was on the list that went out in the media.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from learning that his name was on the list in the media when this happened, did any information come to you after that indicating that the media was wrong?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as you sit here today, you believe -- do you believe that General Mladic -- excuse me, General Miletic was on that list supporting General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry. I took us a diversion from our intercept, but -- so let's get back to it. So you've told us that you believe Mladic was probably at the western front. Then the next person he asks for is -- or, actually, excuse me, President Karadzic says: "You don't know when he's coming back, right?" And you say: "No, I don't." And then you offer General Tolimir, and that's going to be on page 2 of the B/C/S, I'm told. So you may -- yeah, you've got it there. Thank you. And then Karadzic tells you to put him on, and then we get Tolimir on the line, and he apparently puts Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Krajisnik on the speaker phone. And they all have a big chat about General Smith, and they say he's a bit cheeky, and I don't need to go into the whole rest of the conversation, but did you stay on the line and listen to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That'll cut things short. You had mentioned this little initials for archives, archiving things. When did you leave the Main Staff? You were there after the war for a while, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when did you actually leave or retire?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of August 1996 is when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. When -- and at that time that you left, where were the archives that these -- the materials we saw? I think they were the convoy requests. Where were the general Main Staff archives for war? Clearly the war was over by August 1996.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, because, we've never -- you may know, we've never really been able to find the archives. We have a few bits and pieces of original documents. We found January through April of those UN reports, but May, June, July, were not in the Banja Luka archives. Have you any idea where the Main Staff archives went?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. No, I don't have any idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, thank you very much for your time. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic, do you have a redirect? Can you give us an estimate of how long you expect to question the witness, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have an idea of how long you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was not receiving a translation of your words earlier. That's why I did not reply. I'm sorry. May I start, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd like to know beforehand so - for planning purposes - how long you think you will be putting questions to your witness on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sure I will be finished before our first break. I think I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Take your time, and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir. Over the past three days, you've said a lot; and in my re-examination, I would like to go back to some of the issues that were touched upon in order to clarify them. You have spoken a lot about the term "standing in" for somebody in the command post, and you said that in the absence of the commander and the Chief of Staff, the person who stands in for the commander of the Main Staff is either one of his assistants, and you said it would be the assistant for morale, religious matters, and legal matters. You also mentioned the assistant commander for intelligence and security, the assistant commander for logistics, the chief of the sector for development and finance, the chief of the sector for airforce, and the assistant commander for organisation and mobilization. My question to you, sir, is this: When after the commander and of the Chief of Staff there is none of the aforementioned officers, who would be the person to stand in for the commander in the command post in his absence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question properly, if there is no single assistant, you are asking me about that situation. General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Further on, I would like to clarify one more thing. It seems to me that in answering the Prosecutor's question, the Prosecutor said that in that case he was the commander of the military. My question to you is this: When he stands in for him in the command post, what powers does any person standing in for the commander have?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The powers are relative to the organisational work in the command post. The command of the army is still within the purview of the commander if the commander is in the territory of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Court please produce Exhibit number P3923.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The document will appear on e-court on your screen, sir. In the preamble of this document, it says that the unit in question is a company of the 16th Krajina Motorised Brigade and that that unit was engaged in the composition of the 1st Zvornik Brigade. We know that it was during the period between the 16th of July and the 21st of July. Tell me, please, this unit from the 1st Krajina Corps, was it resubordinated to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did, and how, the Zvornik Brigade report about the developments in its zone of responsibility? Did it report to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade sent its reports to the command of the Drina Corps, and the Drina Corps command in its turn sent its unified report for the corps to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could this unit in any shape or form independently send reports from that part of the front line to the Main Staff, and to be more specific, to General Miletic at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would the Drina Corps, reported about in the daily reports from the Zvornik Brigade, would that contain the information on -- that the Main Staff and the -- and General Miletic knew about the developments in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not separately for the Zvornik Brigade, but for the corps, which implies all the brigades of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have not understood each other properly. I'm absolutely clear that those were unified reports of all the brigades, but what I am asking is this: What the Zvornik Brigade told the Drina Corps about the developments in its zone, was that conveyed to the Main Staff by the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should have been part of the report, but whether it was or whether it wasn't, I really can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And to cut the long story short, let's say that the Drina Corps was the one who informed the Main Staff about the developments in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce 5D1194. This is page 19 in the Serbian version and page 11 in the English version. Could we please stay on the first page in the Serbian version just for a moment, the first page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you see that this is the rules of official correspondence and office operations in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we go to page 19 in the Serbian version and page 11 in English. I apologise. Page 19 in Serbian. Both pages are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, yesterday in answering the Prosecutor's questions, you spoke about the abbreviation "SR," and you said that you did not encounter that in your practice and that this does not exist in these rules of office -- operations and official correspondence. Could you please look at paragraph 21. It is actually Article 21; I apologise. In the Serbian version, the text spills over to the following page, page 20. Very well. As you are reading this article on signing documents, do you see this abbreviation "SR" anywhere?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that this did not exist in these rules, and as we are looking at the rules we can actually see that -- or, rather, we can't see it anywhere. It doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce document number P2517.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 28393, line 5, there was some confusion. The Prosecutor asked you, and I quote: "What opinion did the staff have about the proposal put forth by General Tolimir to bomb the refugee columns" -- I apologise -- "to destroy the columns in order to force the Muslims to surrender? Was that based on the opinion of the staff?" Last paragraph, end of quote. Your answer was this: "They did not have any comment to that." My question to you is this: On the 21st of July, were you at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with this situation entitled "Situation in Zepa"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you in the Main Staff act upon the proposal that was put forth by General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not, and there was no way for us to act upon that. Only the person with effective command of a unit that was in a position to act upon this proposal could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would you have carried out a proposal of this sort, and I'm talking about paragraph 4, the first paragraph below paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it was not customary to act upon proposals. You acted upon orders issued by your superiors. He could have proposed anything. He could have proposed for us to use an atomic bomb for all we cared, because we did not have it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would you have acted in the same what when it came to the destruction of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never our goal, the civilian population --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, asked and answered. It's not the operations people, as he said, to act on proposals like this. We know what they do with proposals, and he's already said. So this is going over ground that is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Shall we proceed with your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were there any comments on this text at all, if you will allow me that question.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found it ridiculous, preposterous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think -- I am loathe to ask you this, but given when I asked the witness about this that he had no comment, I would like to reserve the possibility at the end of the redirect to question him on it. I hope I won't need to, but I think in this kind of a context, when he won't answer me about it and will answer the other person about it, I should be able to ask again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see to that if the need arises. Let's continue, Mr. Petrusic. Perhaps you have heard -- Mr. Obradovic, you have heard what Mr. McCloskey had to say. Do you have an explanation why you answered Mr. Petrusic one way and Mr. McCloskey another for -- to the same question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait. Have you received interpretation or not? I am waiting for your answer, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that you were giving the floor to Mrs. Fauveau. That's why I did not answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I gave the floor to you. I couldn't have been addressing Ms. Fauveau saying what you are supposed to have answered. You answered the same question put to you both by Mr. McCloskey and by Mr. Petrusic differently. Why is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether the question was the same. My comment to this is superfluous. It's not necessary. And as to the intentions of General Tolimir, as part of his report on the situation in Zepa, it all doesn't make sense. He was the assistant commander, and he seems to be sending a proposal to his subordinate. This is not a part of military doctrine, and this is really a very confusing document. It's just not soldierly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, when you were asked by Mr. McCloskey yesterday as to that -- in relation to that paragraph, the question was like this: "Was that given due consideration by the staff, that last paragraph?" And your answer was: "I see that. They had [Realtime transcript read in error, "We have"] no comment." But today you said: "We," "We found it ridiculous." So whether there was any discussion at all or it was your personal observation, but you said "we," so if you could expand on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was my personal comment, but I should not have used the pronoun "we." The question was: "Did you comment?" So it came as an automatic answer, but this document was not binding upon us in the staff. In the first three paragraphs, it speaks about the situation; then in the fourth, it provides an opinion of several people, because it says "we are of the opinion." I suppose it conveys another person's -- or several persons' meaning, and then it says: "The most convenient means would be..." this and that. And finally, in the final paragraph, he again provides an opinion of a group. When it comes to acting upon this proposal, that is within the purview of the person who has the power of commanding and decision-making. That's why I am finding all this a bit unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my intention was precisely to clarify the ambiguity and the confusion that was caused by the witness' answer yesterday, and primarily the question that was put to the witness. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, Ms. Fauveau, do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Apart from the fact that the last words uttered by my colleague have not been recorded, and we feel that the answer provided yesterday was not translated very clearly, and we would like this to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Petrusic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, today the Prosecutor showed you an intercept and before that reminded you of an intercept that you spoke about to me on the 17th of November. And on page 28294, this was about Exhibit 1281D, and you commented on a conversation between General Miletic and General Nicolai.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 28294 of the transcript where you commented that conversation and said that General Miletic was in no position to take decisions about such requests submitted by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit P191, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I believe that here, too, there was confusion. On page 28399, the question was, in line 13: "Can you see the part where Morillon is mentioned?" Your answer was: "Yes, but this says pass on to UNPROFOR the request to deploy an officer of the rank of colonel from the Sarajevo sector." And in this next paragraph, it says: "Point out to them" - UNPROFOR - "that we don't want them to send generals, as we have information that they want to misuse" -- "misuse his presence, according to the same scenario under which the presence of General Morillon in Srebrenica was misused." And then the answer continues: "So they are here, and it should be" -- "it should be prevented that this person be a general, but, rather, someone of the rank of colonel." The next question of the Prosecutor was: "I agree. Did you do that, or did you know anyone from the Main Staff who did that?" Your answer was: "I didn't draft requests to UNPROFOR. It was Colonel Milos Djurdjic who was responsible for contacts with UNPROFOR." The Prosecutor's question was: "Well, then, General Miletic would have been working with Djurdjic on that?" Your answer was: "Yes." Do you remember -- no, I withdraw the question. My question after this quotation is: Which business did you mean when you said: "I didn't draft requests to UNPROFOR. It was Colonel Milos Djurdjic"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, there is no business mentioned. The context of that question was clear. It was related to the general or a colonel coming. I don't know what business he's speaking about, but I think he needs to stay within the context of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a question of translation, Mr. Petrusic? Is it a question of interpretation, or do you have to say anything by way of comment to what Mr. McCloskey has just raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comment, but I was referring to the answer or, rather, the questions and answers that the witness provided on page 28399, and I believe that he was mis-lead during that interrogation. He was speaking about Colonel Djurdjic in a completely different context and his business or his tasks, and the Prosecutor is linking that with General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. There are certain limits. The moment you go beyond those limits, you shouldn't be addressing the Chamber in the way that the witness can hear or can follow. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's about the third time there's been such a comment that there is confusion or that -- and now that comes personally to me, so I would ask that to stop and so that it's not, you know, going to affect this witness, who's, I think, you know, doing his best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Let's proceed. Yes, what are we waiting for?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question is, what business or tasks did you mean when you mentioned Colonel Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Colonel Djurdjic was working on the tasks of receiving a fax to requests for the passage of convoys and that he writes approvals or refusals based on the orders of the staff of General Mladic. And those documents, as information notes, are signed by General Miletic, as Colonel Djurdjic is not authorised to sign such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please, look at this document. It is addressed to General Gvero or General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the military hierarchy and in the chain of command at the Main Staff, in the absence of the commander and Chief of Staff, which one of the two -- these two generals would have dealt with this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document 699 -- sorry, P699.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this manual that you can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you work in accordance with this manual at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please page 58 of the Serbian version, and in the English version, it is page 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which methods are applied? Are there any methods?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The full method, the shortened method, and the method without the consultation of organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us the full method?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The full method is applied when enough time is available and the decision-making process is made in accordance with this manual and in line with this method so that the commander with the inner circle of command acquaints them with the situation, makes an assessment of the situation; they formulate a basic idea, which is then passed on to the organs of the command, which, based on this basic idea, says that the factors of armed combat within their purview, and they prepare the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know under which of these methods Directive Number 7 was passed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, because there's no base of the question, because the witness wasn't present during the production of Directive number 7; and the second, there is no evidence that Directive Number 7 was produced in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, being present, doesn't exclude, necessarily, possible knowledge of what went on. So let's proceed, of course, naturally, if he's in a position to answer, because if he's not in a position to answer he will tell us. Yes, Mr. Obradovic, can you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was not present. I didn't take part in the drafting of Directive 7 or Directive 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that you had an opportunity to see Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that you know about the briefings about combat readiness at the Main Staff that took place somewhere in January 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The analysis of combat readiness was made on the 28th and 29th of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From what you know about the analyses of combat readiness, do these analyses include discussions of future tasks of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conclusions are drawn from any analysis and guidelines for further action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The tasks of the army of Republika Srpska, are they put forward by the commander of the army of Republika Srpska based on these analyses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Supreme Command, the political organs, and the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska take part in these analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are the corps commanders present at such analyses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the commander of airforce and anti-aircraft defence as well as the commanders of military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please produce document 5P1394. This is an untranslated document, so I ask for the apologies of the Court. Let us stick to page 1 where there is an -- an illegible stamp bearing the date 28 January 1995; and the title, written in Cyrillic script, we see "The Command of the Drina Corps"; below that, centred, "Analysis"; and below that, "of the combat readiness of the Drina Corps about the elements of combat readiness for the year 1994." Let us please turn to page 19 now. That's the last-but-one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is that the combat readiness for 1994 or 1995? It's a little unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 1 of this analysis, it says: "Analysis of combat readiness of the Drina Corps according to the elements of combat readiness for the year 1994." Below that, there is a date, January 1994 -- 1995, that is. On the next page, in e-court, let us scroll down, please, so that we may see the bottom part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, can you see the first heading, "Basic tasks in the year 1995"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does that refer to the tasks of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Above that, you will see the heading: "Conclusion about combat Readiness of DK for the year 1994." And below that, the tasks for 1995 are listed. Please read out to us task number 4.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The corps command is to find solutions for the full sealing-off of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, and the commands of the brigades shall plan the improvement of their tactical positions and realise them if there should be an interruption of the cease-fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you see this heading in larger type, which reads: "At the level of the Main Staff and the Supreme Command, take care of the following:"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please read out item 1 to us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Solutions will be found for the elimination of enclaves. We see two ways of going about this, either by militarily defeating enemy forces in the enclaves or by political and diplomatic means."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do all corps commands make their analyses before the analysis of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the procedure is as follows: The brigade commands, the regiment commands, the commands of independent battalions and artillery battalions at the end of the current year make analyses of combat readiness for that year, and this is a -- the foundation. These reports are made in two copies, one of which is passed on to the corps command, and at the corps command the analysis of combat readiness is prepared at corps level. After the analyses at corps level are done, the analysis of combat readiness for the past year is made for the entire military in the presence of the political and military leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You're saying "political." Do you mean by that the commander-in-chief, Mr. Karadzic, too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that process of analysis, the corps commanders are present too?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so I said. All corps commanders, the commander of the airforce and anti-aircraft defence, and the commanders of military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do these commanders report to the commander-in-chief and the command of the Main Staff about the events in their zones and their -- and about their tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analysis is made on the plans that are made by the administration for ops at the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please make a break and start over again. We cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, there is a problem with your testimony and the interpreters. The interpreters would like you to go all over again through your answer, please. You had started: "The analysis is made on the plans ..." Can you continue from there, please, and slowly, as slowly as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to the interpreters. The analysis of combat readiness for the past year at the level of the military of the Republika Srpska is made in accordance with the plan which is made by the administration for -- for ops and training. That plan envisages a time-frame for the commander of the Main Staff for his introductory address; and after that, in line with the sequence, as appropriate, the corps commanders, the commander of the airforce and anti-aircraft defence, and the commander of the military schools centre, as well as the organs of the command of the Main Staff, put forward the most important elements of the combat readiness of their respective units and their conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does the commander of the Drina Corps put forward tasks during that analysis at the Supreme Command about the analysis of combat readiness? Does the Drina command -- Drina Corps commander put forward the tasks that he had received or that he had formulated in the framework of the analysis of the combat readiness of his own corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like any other commander, there is no reason for the commander of the Drina Corps not to do what everybody else is also doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So do the corps commanders know best how to assess their own forces, and do they know their capabilities for the coming period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The analysis is made based on the assessment of the enemy forces, your own forces, the area, and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to go back to another document. It will not take long, so I don't know if we should take the break now. I would like to go back to the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on how long you will -- it's not a question of what you would like to deal with. How long? If you're going to finish within five minutes, we can have the break afterwards. If you are not going to finish in five minutes, then I suggest we have the break now and continue later. But take your time. I am not restricting you in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I prefer taking the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's what we will do. We will have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Take your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can the Court please produce Exhibit P5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were talking about this document already. This is Directive 7. You have spoken about the method of the work of the commands. When this directive was passed, did this imply a team work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me just be very precise. We are talking about the full method of team work, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, team work method is involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you had an occasion to see this directive already. You have familiarised yourself with it, and according to the rules and regulations on the working of the commands staff that you also acted upon, could you tell us whether this directive comprises several elements?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who is it who draws up the elements that go into the directive? You don't have to give us any names.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command organs. Every command organ draws up elements pertaining to their respective scope of work or sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Petrusic. Earlier on when the witness was -- when the witness was asked about the method, he answered that he wasn't present at the time. So whether these answers are speculation on the part of the witness, so could you clarify with the witness, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you've heard the Judge's comment, Judge Kwon's comment. Let's just clarify this issue. When you are talking about the methodology or method, can you tell us what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood you was that you were asking me in general terms about methodology. I did not think that you were asking me about the specific methodology of the drafting of this directive. And then you asked me about its contents, and I said that it contains several elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the method used in drafting a directive, and we're talking about the full method here, would this be identical for every single directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since directives are the documents issued by the superior commands or the highest of commands, they are written in situations that allow for ample time for their drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I believe we can move on. You have also told us that the command organs drew up parts of the orders, each of them pertaining to their own respective sector bearing in mind the instruction on the work of the commands and staffs. Could you tell us, who is it who formulates that document that we call "directive"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is formulated based on the proposals put forth before the commander and the proposals which were approved by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, would that be just the technical processing of the elements of the directive that were already formulated?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the elements provided by the command organs that were approved by the commander, the operative organs draw up a whole, a whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, and according to what you know was happening in 1995, who was head of the operations organ that was drawing up the final draft?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the chief of operations in training, General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, both of you. You are overlapping. Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one qualification. This is related in general or particular document, because in question posed by learned colleague Petrusic, he says: "Who is drawing up the final drafts?" What does he mean, this Directive number 7 or in general? It's not clear from the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Could you clarify that with the witness, please, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation may have been, because my question was about the organisation and technical processing of a directive or the directive --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You've already answered that, but...

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The administration for operations and training, i.e., the operations organ, was the one that merged all the elements that had been drafted by the other command organs and put them together in a single document called a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You've also told us that the chief of the administration for operations and training in 1995 was --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: -- General Miletic. You had occasions in 1995 to see the directive. What you saw, did it aberrate in any way from the method that you have spoken about today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to see the method from the document. The document was an integral piece of writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was General Miletic a member of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. If you could bear with me, Your Honours. Mr. President, this brings the examination-in-chief of General Obradovic to an end. General, sir, I would like to thank you for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Petrusic. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to put just one question to this witness about something that was raised by Mr. Petrusic in his additional questions and concerns the role of General Gvero in some activities relative to the document drafted on the 25th of July, if I may I have the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we hear the question so that we can decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I wanted to ask the General whether he had any information that General Gvero had done anything with regard to the document that was received and addressed to him and General Miletic. That was all I wanted to ask the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And no objection from Mr. Petrusic. Yes, go ahead. And we wish to make it clear, this should not be considered as a precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, we are not by this conceding that anyone can stand up and put questions at this stage. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Obradovic, wait for my question, please. With regard to the document that was sent to Generals Miletic and Gvero, do you have any information that General Gvero acted upon that document at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document number is P191.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I don't have it on the screen, I hope that it is a document addressed to either General Gvero or General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The question was not about anybody acting upon this document, and if they did, who was it who acted upon it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your answer was hypothetical, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the nature of the question. I said I didn't know. I never spoke about anybody acting upon this document at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's the end of it. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's a handwriting in the right corner that just says "recipe acknowledged." Perhaps the General can tell us if he recognises the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Obradovic, do you recognise the handwriting in the corner up there of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't. The time is indicated here as 0530, and the inscription is in capital letters, so it's very hard for me to tell whose handwriting this is. It's impossible. And there is no initial; there is no signature. All it says here is "receipt acknowledged."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That brings your testimony to the end, unless my colleagues have got questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a quick question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it is somewhere in the record, but could you tell me the exact title of General Miletic in 1995 again, please? Chief of...

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Miletic was the chief of administration for operations and training at the staff of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, we don't have any further questions for you. Your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, my colleagues, I should like to thank you for having accepted to come over and give testimony, which lasted a few days. And on behalf of everyone, I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I take this opportunity, if you will allow me, to apologise to the interpreters for making their life harder with my speed and inaccuracies in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I am sure they appreciate your statement. Documents. Mr. Petrusic, a list has been circulated, of which I think there is only one document that has not yet been translated. That's the penultimate one, 5D1394. Any objections? Let's start with the other Defence teams. No objection. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So all these documents are admitted, bar the one I just referred to a minute ago, which will remain marked for identification purposes pending translation thereof. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was a problem with the interpreting in B/C/S, but I think it's been solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If there is still a problem, please let me know. THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at the moment when Ms. Fauveau stood up, our interpretation was resumed, so now we are receiving interpretation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Prosecution. There are no other documents to be tendered by any of the other Defence teams, correct? So that brings me to you, Mr. McCloskey. You have circulated a revised list, which contains six documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and in particular the last -- it is my understanding in discussing with Ms. Fauveau the last three intercepts, she did not have an objection to; and therefore, I am offering those into evidence because she's -- well, partly because they're not objecting. And I'm also, as you can see, offering Directive 6 into evidence, and I just wanted to point out, as I had mentioned in my questioning, there was a reference to Directive 6 in Directive 7 which I failed to bring out through the witness. And I just want -- and that Directive 6 is 65 ter 3919, but if we go to Directive 7, which is 65 ter number 5, page 14 in the English, paragraph 6.1, and under "Moral and Psychological Support," we go right underneath the paragraph that you are familiar with about restricting or reducing the logistics, support, and humanitarian aid. And the sentence right below that is: "In the implementation of other forms of support for combat operations, all measures are to be taken according to Directive Operation number 6."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Any objections? None. So all are admitted. The last one, it's still not yet translated, 3924, 65 ter 3924, so that one will be MFI'd pending translation thereof. All right. Is the next witness ready, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hope the witness is available, Your Honour. Out of an abundance of caution, I think it would perhaps be prudent to inform the witness of his rights according to Rule 90(e).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Before you start your testimony as a Defence witness for General Miletic, you are required to make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the whole truth. Madam Usher is handing you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you understand English at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to be using the Serbian language, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but how much English do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you do know something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very superficially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Before you start giving evidence, I need to draw your attention to a special provision which we have in our rules, and it is the following: There are going to be a lot of questions put to you, both by the Defence team for General Miletic and by others, including the Prosecution. There is a possibility - I am not saying that this will happen - but there is a possibility that some questions may be put to you, which, if you answer truthfully, could possibly incriminate you and, therefore, expose you to possible criminal proceedings against you. As I said, I am not sure that this is going to happen, but if it does, happen our rules provide some protection to you. You can, in such instances, if you feel that by answering such questions you could incriminate yourself, you could ask us to exempt you from answering such questions. This is a limited right. It's a qualified right. It's not absolute, in other words. We are at liberty, after considering everything, to grant you such an exemption, and we are also entitled to force you to answer the question. If we force you to answer the question, there are some further -- there is some further protection provided by our rules. The protection is as follows: If you answer truthfully such questions when you are forced to answer them, then whatever you say, which is incriminatory, cannot be used against you in any proceedings - criminal proceedings - that could be taken against you here or elsewhere. Have you understood what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have been clear enough, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who will be leading? Yes, Ms. Fauveau, lead counsel for General Miletic, will start first. Go ahead, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you give us your name and first name, please?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Novica Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about your education and the degrees that you have earned?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I completed the elementary school and grammar school in Sarajevo, and after that, the four-year academy in Belgrade in Banja Luka, the two-year academy in Belgrade, and the National School of Defence; that lasted for one year in Belgrade as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before continuing, I would ask you to please slow down a bit; otherwise, the interpreters will have slight difficulties.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What were your functions before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I was the commander of a platoon of a company; I was the deputy commander of a battalion; I was the battalion commander; I was the desk officer in the operations organ of a brigade; the assistant chief of staff for operations and training in a brigade; and, finally, the chief of staff of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When did you join the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I joined the army of Republika Srpska on the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what were your functions at the time when you joined the army?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: When I joined the army of Republika Srpska, I was still the chief of staff in an anti-armour brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you now tell us what were your functions within the army of the Republika Srpska from the 12th of May, 1992, all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I have not received any translation. Besides being the Chief of Staff of a brigade, I was also the commander of a brigade, the commander of a tactical group that consisted of several brigades, and I was the commander of the East Bosnia Corps. And after the war, I was the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, which was then renamed as the 3rd Corps. I was the deputy chief of the General Staff, and I was the chief of the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. I was pensioned off in 2002 with the rank of Colonel General.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said you were the commander of the East Bosnian Corps. Was that your function in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And who was your immediate superior when you were commander of the East Bosnian Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: My superior was the commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And who at the time was the chief of the staff of the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And during what time-period did General Milovanovic exercise that function as chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And since when have you known General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Since 1993, when he was appointed the chief of operations and training organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know what was the function -- or the functions of General Miletic in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of the ops and training administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you were appointed commander of the East Bosnian Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I was ordered to take over that post on the 31st of August, 1992. I believe that the order arrived on the 1st or the 2nd of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the East Bosnian Corps have another commander before you?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Before me, yeah. The commander was Colonel Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know why you replaced Colonel Ilic in these functions?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: No. Somebody from the Main Staff should answer that. Probably, they were dissatisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know to what position or what functions General Ilic was appointed when you became commander of the corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: He was in the same function that later was taken over by General Miletic. He was the chief of the ops and training administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that perhaps the Main Staff was not satisfied with General Ilic and that he may have left to take up other duties as head of the operations and training department. Did those new duties, were they of a higher rank or a lower rank than those that he had beforehand?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: In the army, that's called formational rank. The formational rank of a corps commander was higher than that of the chief of the ops and training administration so that Colonel Ilic was appointed to a lower-ranking function.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that in 1995 your direct superior was Commander Ratko Mladic. Can you say which were the people who had the authority to give you orders in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, General Mladic gave me orders, the commander of the Main Staff, and in his absence it was his deputy, the Chief of Staff, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the civilian authorities also have this authority?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you document 5D1003. You said that the civilian authorities did not have the authority to give you orders, but were there situations in which that could happen, nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is a document pointing out disrespect of the hierarchical structure of the military in which all orders or requests to the corps, as subordinate to the Main Staff, should have gone through the Main Staff. So that the commander-in-chief, if he so wanted, or the Ministry of Defence should have directed their orders or requests through the Main Staff. This is pointing out this fact and warning against the repetition of such -- such a procedure. There were attempts by the civilian bodies to exert influence on the commands of corps and of brigades, but we resisted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that you "resisted that," are you speaking about your particular corps, the East Bosnian corps, or more generally of the entire army?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: That was probably the case elsewhere, too, because I heard at briefings that other peoples were facing similar problems as me. There was a situation that since the state of war hadn't been declared, it was impossible to abide by the rules governing law and humanitarian law. So there were problems with the units that were composed of people from different municipalities so that some would receive their salaries and others wouldn't, and so huge problems arose in the military. And those who paid out the salaries considered that that gave them the automatic right to influence personnel matters - who should be commander, et cetera - and they were also trying to turn the units into local units, which would have been extremely detrimental because we wouldn't have been able to use them elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you slow down a little bit, please, in your answer. In other words, speak slower, more slowly, okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm a soldier. I'm not used to speaking slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you had direct contact with President Karadzic as commander of the corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Rarely, I believe only once or twice. It was at meetings where combat readiness was analysed and when there were other people present too.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the fact that President Karadzic tried occasionally to give orders directly to the corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: There were such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document 5D1167.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here, you see an order of the staff -- or a document of the staff conveying an order of President Karadzic, and what I'm interested in is point 3. That is on the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you look at this order, this document was addressed to your corps, among others. How would you interpret what is written here? How do you understand it?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: That was a time of crisis. I believe that those in power feared a military coup or something, and that's why the commander-in-chief ordered -- issued such an order, which was passed on to us. But this is a political thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if we look at point 4, it reads: "[In English] I forbid all command levels to make any amendments to approve decisions and issue orders without my approval." [Interpretation] What I would like to ask you is, as a general rule, when you would receive an order from your superior, was it possible for you to amend such an order, to change it in any way?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, a commander receives a general order with a general task, and it is up to him to determine ways and means of implementing it. Likewise, during combat, various surprises are possible which entail amendments to a decision. This is not appropriate with regard to both military terminology and the way the military acts.
