This is an exclusively political document, the intention of which is probably to preserve the situation in the battlefield as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Throughout the course of the war, were there other situations in which documents or orders handed down by President Karadzic were passed on to the corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but mostly they went through the Main Staff, and we received documents informing us that these were conveyed. Among them, there were decisions of the Assembly or the decisions of the Supreme Defence Counsel, and the Main Staff would receive these from the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to now focus a bit on the organisation of the corps command, the command of the East Bosnian Corps. Can you tell us what bodies made up the command structure of the East Bosnian Corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The East Bosnian Corps consisted of the command and the subordinate units. The command included the commander; the first down was the Chief of Staff who was also his deputy; and then there were the commander's assistants, who together with the Chief of Staff made up this command component; and below the Chief of Staff, there was his staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And which entity made up the staff of the East Bosnian Corps, which entities?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The staff of the East Bosnian Corps differed from the staff at the Main Staff, because we were an operational unit [as interpreted], and the Main Staff is a strategic command. The operational organ of the corps included the intelligence organ, the personnel organ; whereas, at the Main Staff those were immediately subordinate to the commander. They were not subordinate to the staff. At the staff of the East Bosnian Corps, there were -- there was also an ops organ and the chiefs of services.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that on page 46, line 20, there is a mistake, because instead of having the operational organs of the corps, I think one should be talking about the staff of the corps. I can clarify this with the witness if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you talked about the body in charge of security and internal affairs, can you tell us where these bodies were as far as your corps is concerned? I wasn't talking about security, but intelligence.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The intelligence organ was part of the staff, and when we're talking about the Main Staff, it was different there. There was a separate organ for intel and security, which was subordinate to the commander of the Main Staff; whereas, at the corps command, the intelligence organ was subordinate to the Chief of Staff of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in your corps, how did you interact with the body in charge of internal affairs -- in charge of personal affairs?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: It was through the Chief of Staff. I understood you. I understood the question. They were subordinate to the Chief of Staff, and through the Chief of Staff I can -- I communicated with them. Exceptionally, there was direct communication. But in principle, the Chief of Staff was in charge of them because they were organs of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who inside the East Bosnian Corps gave the orders to the staff -- to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was my deputy, and I issued him orders, and he issued orders to his staff. That is normal procedure in a military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How did you let the higher command, i.e., the Supreme Commander, know about what you were doing on a daily basis inside your corps? I didn't talk about the Supreme Command but the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: You're right. I reported to the Main Staff; that is, I was subordinate to it. I didn't report to the Supreme Command. It was the Main Staff that reported to the Supreme Command; that is in accordance with the rules of subordination that had to be respected. All orders issued by the command of the East Bosnian Corps were signed by me, anything that was passed on to the Main Staff, irrespective of the fact from which where it originated. Exceptionally, in my stead, the Chief of Staff could sign, or the operational duty officer in case both of us were at the front line, and some telegram has to be dispatched immediately, and we were familiar with its content.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you talk to us a little bit about the way in which you prepared your reports. What did you have at your disposal, and how did you prepare these reports?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is daily reporting and periodical reporting. Daily reporting takes place on a daily basis. At 1900 hours, a report is dispatched about the events in the past 24 hours, and it's sent to the commander of the Main Staff. That report arrives at his staff. And periodical reports are monthly reports, quarterly reports, semi-annual reports, and annual reports. The annual report is called "The analysis of combat readiness", and it is made for an entire year. To make such a report -- or to build such a report, let me just explain for the daily report. The daily report is made based on the reports from subordinate units, which are sent an hour earlier to the ops centre of the corps. That report is then made. The entire situation in the area of the corps is summarised, and that report is signed by either the Chief of Staff or myself. Depending on who was present at the moment. In principle it was me, because with our signature we assume responsibility for the accuracy of that report, and it is passed on to the Main Staff encrypted. Apart from that, we were in phone contact with the commander daily.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we clarify, a -- the daily reports which you sent off. How accurate was information you received from your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: We carried out inspections. I cannot say for any instance that it was a hundred per cent accurate, but every day there was a team from the corps command inspecting a unit to check the situation, and it was in the position to verify the information received one day earlier, so that we reduced the likelihood of false reports because that can be very dangerous sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that you cut down on false reports. What would have happened if you had not sent off those teams of men to the subordinate units every day?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: They would otherwise have depicted the situation as much more favourable, and I might have been in the position to go to enemy territory, because I would have believed them to be somewhere where they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that these false reports do have fairly adverse effects. Could you explain this a little bit? What happens when a false report comes in from a brigade or elsewhere? To be quite clear, I would like to submit this to you: In a situation where you are not aware of the fact that the report is false.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I am not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, because there was a fault in the interpretation, or interruption. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that these false reports may have adverse effects. What I would like to know when false information comes in and it reaches your corps and you don't know that this information is false, what happens then?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I depends on the effects that can be produced. If we are talking about small lies, it is not as series, but the consequences can be disastrous, and you don't know until you find out. In every army there must be inspection; likewise, every report is checked in order to prevent such situations. A minute ago I made a jocular remark, but there were situations when some commanders, due to false reports that their forces had reached, say, a hill, upon going -- or after going to that hill, the commander would be caught prisoner by the enemy. Hence, the inaccuracy and timeliness of reporting is extremely important in the military. That is why there is the staff organ that does that, and everybody from the command carries out these inspections along all lines, because it does matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We'll get there. A while ago, when I interrupted you, I believe you were talking about the contacts you had with your commander. Could you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, apart from written reports, every evening, from roughly 2000 to 2100 hours, we were in phone contact with the commander of the Main Staff or the Main Staff. Then, he would sometimes demand explanations, and sometimes he commended us, but sometimes he would also reprimand us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that you were in contact on a daily basis with the commander. Can you tell us who contacted whom? Was it he who contacted you or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: About that report, he contacted us. We were waiting for him to call us. It was our duty. We also had the right to call him whenever there was an extraordinary situation and when we wanted to inform him of something, not -- without waiting for the daily report because it was too important and to ask for approval for some of our decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where he was calling you from?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Most times, he would call from the room where they held their regular meetings where they discussed the reports received from the corps -- corps, but if he was absent, we would be in contact with him for -- from wherever he was. If he was in our zone of responsibility, it would go through our communication lines. Anyway, the occasions when we did not communicate with the commander daily were very rare.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To clarify something, when he was not at the Main Staff and when he was not in your area but with the 1st Krajina Corps, how did he reach you, then, in that case?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I have to say that it sometimes happened that General Milovanovic would call up, and he would talk, and then the commander would call again, and he would also talk. He would most often communicate by direct line with the command of that corps with the Main Staff, and the Main Staff would then include us, because they had the possibility of putting us through individually or several of us together.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show you document 5D1004. We are still talking about reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could just anybody come to the corps and ask what is happening inside the corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course not. It's not a railway station. It's a staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this document, those people entitled to receive the reports are named. Why was such a report necessary according to you?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether they were paying attention, but I said that even municipalities were trying to exert an influence and demanded that brigade commanders report to them concerning the problems and the situation bypassing the corps command, but they were not authorised to do so. So this was a document aimed as preventing any attempts to impinge on the unity of the army and the chain of command, and this all happened because no state of war was declared. Had a state of war been declared, the presidents of the municipalities would have been subordinate to the commander, but as it was, the civilian authorities acted independently of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this first paragraph, we can see the names of those people who are entitled to receive these reports. Is General Miletic mentioned here together with the names of other people entitled to do so? In your view, what does the word "subordination" mean?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: To be subordinate is the opposite of to be superior to. The senior person is superior, and the lower-down one is subordinate, which doesn't mean that he's being humiliated in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: A while ago, I put the question to you about the document that is still in front of you, and I asked you whether General Miletic's name is among the names of those peoples entitled to receive the reports. You answered, but your answer was not recorded in the transcript. Could you tell us, please, what your answer was.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I was quite clear. No, he was not among those persons, and he did not have the right to command or to receive orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You are talking about receiving orders or about receiving reports. Which do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The one receiving the reports here has the right to command, and General Miletic was neither one nor the other. He was the professional organ in the staff of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We were talking about subordination. Was this principle abided by in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was abided by.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have already talked about the way in which the reports were sent. I would just like to clarify this. Could the brigade send reports directly to the Main Staff or not?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: No, it couldn't. In the army, they say only exceptionally if the Main Staff set it apart from the corps and commanded it directly, then it would, but otherwise, no. The corps -- the corps command could not be bypassed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D1008. In the meantime, I'd like to say that this is a document that stems from the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska and sent to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I would like you to do is have a quick look at paragraph 2, which is a very short paragraph. Was this principle applied throughout the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This was an exception. This is not the military way of subordination or contacts. Evidently, a commander had gone beyond what was excepted and overstepped his authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned a while ago those analyses conducted relating to combat readiness. At what levels of the command were these analyses conducted?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The analyses were conducted at the tactical, operational, and strategic levels, at the level of brigades, at corps level, and at the level of the Main Staff for the whole army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In 1995 in your corps, were such analyses conducted?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I have to clarify here, Your Honours, that the analysis is first conducted at the lower level. Those analysis are then submitted to the corps. The corps conducts its own analysis and draws up a report, and then that is sent to the Main Staff for an analysis of combat readiness. And then, when it comes to directives, it goes the other way around. The Main Staff delivers this to the corps, and the corps sends it to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer, please, when the orders of the directive arrive and are sent -- by the Main Staff and sent to the corps. What happens to the corps and the brigade after that? I'll repeat --

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I'll [microphone not activated] happy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the Main Staff sends out orders and directives to the corps, what happens after that between the corps and the brigade?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I was not clear enough. I was clear. Reports are sent from the brigade through the corps to the Main Staff, and when the Main Staff sends a directive, it comes to the corps; it is dealt with by the corps; the corps then issues its own orders, which it sends to the brigades. On the basis of this, the brigade has to do the same towards its battalion commands, so the level is lower and lower. And this is the opposite sequence of what happens when we're dealing with analysis and reports. So directives, conclusions, assessments, and orders for further action, those are what is comprised in the directive.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When we talk about combat readiness, analysis at the level of the Main Staff, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, between 1992 and 1995, were such analyses conducted at that level?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether such analyses were conducted in 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I know. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who else was there to conduct this analysis?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: President Karadzic, as the Supreme Commander; the prime minister; the Minister of Defence; and I don't remember who else. From this Supreme Defence Council, there was General Mladic with his associates, and the corps commanders, and the commanders of those units that had direct links to the Main Staff. This happened in Hans Pijesak, to the best of my recollection, in January or February 1995. I know there was still snow on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that General Mladic was there with his associates. Was General Milovanovic there?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I think he was. I think he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D1206. This is an order from the Main Staff dated the 23rd of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document means?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: It's a regular document where the commander is planning an analysis of combat readiness; he's telling us where it will be held, who is to attend, and what we are to prepare, because we bring with us written documents, our own analyses of combat readiness. But the commander is also requesting that we also report orally on certain points according to his selection, and he's giving us time to prepare, because we can't come to that meeting unprepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we have page 2 of this document, please. You can see the date, which is the 30th of January, 1995, and then: In presence -- in the presence of the highest political organs of the Republika Srpska, continue with the analyses of combat readiness as follows. Here, under paragraph (a): [In English] Briefing by the commanders up to ten minutes by following issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you prepare something like this for these analyses?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, I did. How could I come unprepared? I can explain. Shall I?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you explain paragraph (e), which is to be found on page 3 in English -- page 4, I'm sorry. [In English] "... war-waging strategies and peace negotiations and the task of the army and VRS units in carrying out these assignments."

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Every analysis has to analyse what happened over the past years - what were the successes, what were the failures, what can be learned from both - and then the Main Staff and the Supreme Command then define the strategic tasks to be implemented in the forthcoming period. We, the corps commanders, implemented the strategic goals through our operative activities, and the brigade commands did the same at their level at the tactical level. Here, we are asked to give some proposals concerning our own engagement so as to enable this plan of what to do next to be drawn up in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes. When you conducted this analysis, was the plan for the upcoming year mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to assist in clarifying this point. It says here what the commanders are supposed to report on, and then the sector for intelligence and security assesses the situation, and see, it says that the logistics sector provides for the material needs and so on and so forth. But as for defining further goals, it doesn't say who does that. That, however -- well, first of all, there is the Supreme Commander, the Supreme Defence Counsel. They are the most responsible people, and that definition follows from everything that has been heard beforehand, everything that's mentioned here. And then the plan is drawn up for the forthcoming period. That's what I've been trying to explain. This is military terminology. I do apologise. I apologise if you don't understand me, but you can ask me. Quite simply, there are special schools of the military and special schools for judges. So that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, General Miletic? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I see you don't have page 3 on your monitors, and that's what the General is referring to. We are following this in the Serbian version, but you have a different page on your screen. I just wanted to draw attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We can also see it on a different monitor, so don't bother -- don't worry. But thank you for pointing that out. Yes, let's continue, Ms. Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you set forth what was to apply to your corps, what was the most salient item of your presentation, I mean, the presentation you made to your commander?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, every commander puts forward what is peculiar to his area of responsibility, and I did the same. At that period there was a cease-fire on, but in my area, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not respect the cease-fire, and that is what I focussed on. As regards my proposals, I don't know whether you want me to tell you what they were. They were mostly minor corrections of what had to be done in cooperation with the Drina Corps because we had problems with constant enemy attacks on the radio relay intelligence transmitter at the top of Majevica at Stolice, which was crucial for all communications, both military and civilian, between the eastern and western parts of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Your answer, you used the word "proposal." Were you entitled to make proposals on what should be done in the area of responsibility of your corps, in other words, of those actions that were to be undertaken?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Of course. That was how it was done. I had the possibility of making this proposal, but certain things were not approved. Usually 60 per cent of your proposals would be approved and 40 not, and they would add another 60 per cent of their own. But, well, that's military life for you. You understand, sometimes we weren't very eager to take certain action, but the command would force us to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D967.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to ask you whether you are aware of this document. Have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. I've seen it. This is the schedule. It refers to time when certain people would report, but the questions are the same as the ones in the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now turn to page 3 in B/C/S and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see in column 4, on the second line, there are a few abbreviations. Could you explain this to us, please? This is on the last line in English.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is Sunday, from 2200 to 2230 hours, proposals, conclusions, and tasks of the army of VRS, and those who are responsible are chief of the operations and training administration and chief of operations and training in the corps, because I took my operative officer -- my operations officer with me, Colonel Gengo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what the proposal, conclusion, and task for the army of VRS, your unit, in 1995 mean exactly? In other words, can you explain to us the meaning of this particular sentence? What were the tasks of the organ in charge of operations and training as regards this particular task?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: In this case, they were the professional organ who, based on the discussions from the Supreme Commander to the lowest-ranking officers, they would extract the most important points from these discussions and draw a conclusion, and either the Supreme Commander or the chief of the Main Staff, if they accepted what they had drawn up because they would read it in the break, this would be built into the directive, and the directive would be a written document based on this. This is their job. They are the professional organs, but it's more of a secretarial job to draw up a document, because this is not their wisdom. It's the wisdom of those who participated in the discussion. Their task is to put it in military terminology, to streamline it, and to put it in the right shape to be drawn up as a document. So they were doing this secretarial work, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break, I would like to show you another document. This is 5D1208. This is, once again, an order, a document stemming from the Main Staff dated the 16th of February, 1995, which was also sent out to your corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is, again, a request where the superior command is asking for the most recent information for the purposes of planning further actions. They asked for a report on the assessment, certain axes and so on. This is purely military terminology, but it boils down to they are asking for fresh information, the most recent information, more recent than the information provided at the analysis meeting, the analysis of combat readiness meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time when it's convenient to you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have one question about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oui.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Was it customary -- this document was sent out to all the corps. Was it customary that such a request was sent to all the corps at the same time?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are aiming at, but this was sent out to all corps because a general document is made for the entire military, but they could have demanded things from just one corps. It always depends on what you want to achieve, and it depends on the situation. It is usual to send it out to all, even to those who are not concerned, but in order for them to be informed that certain things are being done, et cetera, that's one of the ways of informing others what their neighbours are doing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Merci, madam. Yes, 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, have you ever heard of Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness Exhibit P5. Could we go to page 10 in English and 13 in B/C/S, please. Could we look at the very bottom of the page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like you to clarify some of the tasks entrusted to the East Bosnian Corps in this directive. Would you please look at the last sentence on the page, and then pass on to page 15 in B/C/S. It's all on page 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We see in this directive an operation called Sadjestvo, and we can see that it's a strategic operation. Could you please explain to us what it means when they say that an operation is a strategic-level operation?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: I hope that you noticed my saying at the beginning that there is the tactical level, and a brigade acting is at the tactical level; when several brigades are acting together, then it's at the operational level; and then there is cooperation at the level of the whole state or the community. For an operation to be strategic, it must be conducted by at least two operational units. Exceptionally, it can be only one operational unit if it's of the uppermost importance for the whole country. When two corps are engaged, then the superior command must be included to make -- to facilitate cooperation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could be asked to slow down a little. This is not our daily bread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, the interpreters are having problems. If you could kindly start again and speak more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I am acting as a soldier. I will try to improve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget about that, as a soldier. You are testifying here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Well, perhaps to make things more concise, in order to be strategic, an operation must be conducted by at least two operational units. Exceptionally, it could also be carried out by one single operational unit if it relates to something that is really paramount for the country. Then you began to talk about the fact that when two corps are engaged, then the higher command must be involved. Could you then carry on with your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You interpreted it nicely. Your Honours, a strategic operation is conducted with strategic forces and with a strategic objective, and it is lead by a strategic command, in this case, the Main Staff or the Supreme Command. This particular operation was planned at the strategic level, but due to the events in the western Krajina front and the attack of the forces of the regular units of the Croatian army and the army of BiH against the western Krajina municipalities, this operation was never actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that the operation was planned at the strategic level. Who, then, in fact, planned this operation Sadjestvo?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look further down, we can see that another operation is mentioned, Spreca, and according to this directive it is described as an operational-level operation. Could you explain to us what those terms mean?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is an operation carried out by two corps, the Eastern Bosnian Corps and the Drina Corps, and its objective was to neutralize the forces that were attacking daily the relay station and the top of Majevica. So the objective was to disable those forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier you said that when two corps are involved, that would be a strategic operation. And why, in this case, was it an operational-level operation?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: In this case, not all forces -- not the entire forces of both corps were engaged, only part of the forces. Not even the entire Zvornik Brigade took part on the left wing, only part of its forces, and from my side, only one brigade, the 1st Majevica Brigade took part. And irrespective of the fact the two corps were engaged, there was little depth and small forces, and that's why this was not a strategic operation and it had no strategic significance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And who planned operational-level operations?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, I was tasked to do it. The command of the Eastern Bosnian Corps planned this operation, so it is assigned to one of the corps because the forces employed were not great.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what was the role of the administration responsible for operations and training within the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska in planning operational-level operations?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: They had no role in it whatsoever. It was our job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If you look at the last paragraph regarding the East Bosnian Corps, just above the paragraph concerning the Drina Corps, we can read that it has to do with improving the operative tactical position, and it also mentions camouflage measures, combat activities. Can you tell us what exactly this paragraph is describing? What does it relate to?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will have to use military terminology in my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Demonstrational activities means fake attacks. By doing so, we will keep busy some forces, and the enemy will not know where we will really attack, and so we spread out their forces. The next thing is operational and tactical camouflaging. The first level of this camouflaging is the name of the operation. The operation was called Spreca 95, and the Spreca river has nothing to do with the area where the operation was actually carried out. So if the enemy should hear about the operation and its name and it has a code name, the enemy will not be able to suppose what the real objective of the operation is. The next step is -- to bring units in the preparation area is done according to plan at night, hiding movements, et cetera, in order to -- to have the enemy get a wrong image of what the purpose of our regrouping is. And then there are also false telegrams that are sent out in order to hide our true intentions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And at what tactical strategic or operational level were these actions planned?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Again, I must go into these levels. There is tactical camouflaging, and it starts from camouflaging the soldiers, the vehicles, the positions, the intentions, et cetera, at the tactical level. Then there is operational camouflaging at the higher level of divisions and corps, which is much more complex. And then there is strategic camouflaging to disguise our intentions at the strategical level. It can be done through the media and in various other ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Generally speaking, relating to tactical combat activities, who was responsible for planning those combat activities?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Tactical combat activities are planned and implemented by the commands at tactical levels, that is, the commands of brigades, battalions, companies, down to the platoon level so that everybody has their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when tactical combat activities were carried out in the zone within the responsibility of your corps or planned by the your corps, would the body responsible for operations and training have a role to play in such planning? Speaking of the body in charge of operations and training within the corps.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The ops organ of the General Staff acts in the framework of the General Staff. That doesn't have any remit to plan at the operational level. We can, if necessary, be called upon to conduct an inspection on the ground to see whether everything is done in accordance with the rules, but everybody has their own responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, once again, I would ask you to please speak slowly because, once again, part of your answer has not been recorded, just one part of your answer, but that I'm interested in: The obligations or powers of the organ in charge of operations and training within your corps in the context of combat activities that were planned in one of your brigades.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The ops and training organ of the corps plans operations at operational level that is within the corps, and the brigade command plans at the tactical level, and those are completely separate levels. And the interfering of one with the other cannot be allowed because, thus, responsibility would be reduced also. So that the ops organ of the Main Staff, by sending out a directive has met its obligations regarding the planning of the operation of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. It gets feedback through daily reports or through a final report about the operation after the analysis has been carried out. It's a professional organ. It does not -- it does not monitor the operation, nor does it take part in it at the lower level.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 15 in English and page 21 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This directive is signed by the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, but we can also read on the document that it was drafted by Colonel Miletic. Can you explain to us, in the procedure of drafting such a military document, what does the term "drafted by" mean, this term that we see at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: In civilian terms, you would say "finalised." So he compiled it from elements that he received from the other parts of the Main Staff, the decision taken by the commander, and it was for him to draw up this document, to edit it, technically, with his typists. And if -- if it was necessary to work on a map, then he would have to do that, also, and hand it to the Chief of Staff for inspection, who is then supposed to take it to the commander of the Main Staff; and he was then supposed to go to the Supreme Command with the document, have the president read it, and if he agrees with it, sign it and stamp it with the stamp of the Supreme Command. I can see that this is, indeed, the case here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the Supreme Command of the Republika Srpska have organs that could draft this type of document, such a directive?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the Supreme Command never established such an organ. They didn't have a military cabinet, and so this professional part was left to the professional body, and that is the ops and training department of the General Staff. I must explain. At the strategic level, if the state of war had been declared, the Main Staff would have become the staff of the Supreme Command, but that was never done. And they were even at two different places, which created great problems in communication. Likewise, if the state of war had been declared and all units of the -- then all the units of the Ministry of the Interior would have been placed under a single command. The way things were, they were under the command of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the influence of the person who drafted this act on the content of the act?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: If you mean in the creative sense, then only in linguistic terms and the use of military terminology; otherwise, there was no influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the first page of the -- in B/C/S. I think it's the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What I am interested in is this. Could you look at the date on this document. It's 8th of March, 1995. I would now like to show you the first page in English --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I believe it's page 23 in B/C/S. This is a document by which this was sent to the 1st Krajina Corps. We see the date of the 17th of March, 1995; in other words, approximately ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you tell us why a document of a military nature was sent ten days after the date mentioned on the document in question?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know the reason. It is somewhat surprising. Possibly, there was a dissatisfaction at some level with the way it was drafted, so it was rephrased, or there was nobody to forward it. I can't see any other reason, but these are -- this is all speculation. I was their subordinate. I was not at the Main Staff, so I cannot say why there was such a delay. For the military way of life and the efficiency in commanding, this is too great a delay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How much time elapses between the completion of a deed and its forwarding to the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could just rephrase the question. It's awfully general. It might be more helpful to have some more specificity as to what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In an army, when such documents are dealt with, how urgent is it?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This document should be taken to the recipient within 24 hours by an officer, since this is top secret. So it must be handed personally to a commander. So an officer from the Main Staff has to bring it personally and bring back a receipt. But with regard to the problems with transportation, it was realistic to expect that to happen within three or four days and the condition that one man does it all. But it can also be done faster if you organise differently. This is a huge delay, but I cannot venture to explain it because I want to stick to what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to talk a little bit more extensively about the Sadjestvo operation. You said that this operation was never conducted. You mentioned that it had been planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show you document 5D1209, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, could you tell us what this document is about? What is it all about?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is a list of the documents pertaining to a single plan. The number of pages is mentioned here, each of which has to be verified; the number of pages of a map, which is the -- the map source; and then this document is treated as top secret. So it undergoes special treatment as regards its safekeeping; therefore, all these signatures appear at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before item 7 of this document, we can see that the plan, support plan, intelligence plan, is mentioned, intelligence support plan. Who is usually in charge of the drafting of such a plan?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: That's a professional document, and it's drawn up by the intelligence organ; in this particular case, the sector for intelligence, their -- and security, their intelligence part.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this case, this document shows us a list, which comes from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Which party would have been in charge of compiling such a list?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: The list is compiled by whoever is drawing up the document, the operations organ, that is. As a rule, he also distributes it. This was a rare occasion for General Miletic to leave the Main Staff and visit other corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you document 5D1211. As you can see, this is the intelligence support plan. In the left-hand corner, we can see approved by the commander, and there is a signature there. What does this mean, "approved commander"?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: All documents drawn up in the command are approved by the commander. They are drawn up by professionals who are his subordinates in the Main Staff. This is done by the intelligence administration, and he approved it with his signature. That's his signature, General Mladic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you 5D1210. This is the security support plan. What I am interested in is this, the signature, once again, which is below "approved commander," Colonel Ratko Mladic. We can see a signature here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of General Milovanovic, but up there it says "for the commander." He's the second-ranking person in the Main Staff, and he stands in for the commander or deputises for him and has the right to sign a document in his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who in the command has the authority to approve this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This document and all the kinds of documents are approved by the commander, and in his absence, the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the middle of the page -- or, rather, the title. We can see that Sadjestvo 95 operation is mentioned in this document. This is a name we saw mentioned in Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You are an experienced man in the military. You commanded a corps. You were head of staff in the army. According to you, could somebody approve a document without knowing the basis for which this document was drafted?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, this question goes beyond the military terminology. Anyone who signs a document familiarises himself with it, examines the validity of the document. When he determines the that the document is in good order, he approves it. I don't know how someone could sign something that is not in good order. In that case, he wouldn't approve it, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I will put my question more directly to you. You remember that the operation Sadjestvo 95 was mentioned in Directive 7. Could General Milovanovic have approved the plan for Sadjestvo without knowing the contents of Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: In my view, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would just like you to repeat the answer please, the answer you had just provided.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: In my view, in my opinion, that was not possible. He would have to know about this because how else could he approve the plan? There would be no logic in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We have already discussed the Spreca operation a little. I would now like to address this in greater detail. Do you remember when your corps started to plan this operation?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: My corps started planning this operation when it received the directive. However, Operation Spreca, I had to start carrying out before the directive arrived. The forces of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had one-sidedly violated the cease-fire, suddenly attacked the forces at Majevica, and encircled the repeater at the top of the mountain at Stolice. And I immediately had to engage reserve forces in coordinated action with the forces of the Ministry of the Interior to block their further advance and then to retake the lost positions, and this lasted for about 15 days. In the meantime, the directive and the order for Spreca arrived, and this was but a continuation of what had happened previously. No action would have been planned or implemented had the cease-fire not been violated. At the meeting, it was said if the enemy one-sidedly violates the cease-fire, then an operation has to be planned. We respected the cease-fire. The soldiers relaxed a little bit, and our enemies, the other side, took advantage of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the Main Staff received a specific order relating to Spreca? [In English] Whether the main staff sent a specific order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Along with a directive, we also received a specific order for that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see document 5D972.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, as you can see, this is an order entitled "Combat Order to Carry Out Operation Spreca 95." And then, in the first paragraph, in the preamble, Directive 7 is mentioned. First of all, I would like to know whether you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the order for Operation Spreca. We could not wait for the regular procedure, but something had to be done urgently in order to prevent the action at Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, do you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's General Milovanovic's signature. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the basis of your military experience, again, this document, this order which refers to Directive 7, do you think this could have been drafted without any knowledge of Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC
utterances.text: This operation was an integral part of the directive, and this order was caused by the speeding-up of the preparations for the implementation because of events at the front. How could he have written an order for this operation had he not consulted the directive? It would not have been possible to draw it up without consulting the general document that preceded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I know that there is still one minute to go, but could we stop now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. So we are going to stop here, General, and we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. In the meantime, between now and tomorrow you are not to communicate with anyone on the subject matter of your testimony. Is that clear? Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
